Early reports suggested that the emails came from a Taiwanese email address and were signed by a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan" – a fictitious state or region roughly mapping to "the land of Misogyny," with "vilayat" meaning an administrative region of the Ottoman Empire. Various theories have been reported about the identity of the sender, ranging from a teacher based in the Philippines whose email was compromised to a Russia-backed disruption operation. Neither are confirmed. Russia denied any involvement. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Thursday evening that there was no credence to the emails, and that whoever was behind the coordinated hoax sought to invoke chaos across the country. "To date, there is no evidence of a concrete danger," she said, ANSA reported. "These messages aren't intended to shock, they're intended to scare. "Those who write them are primarily seeking our fear, wasted days, suspicion, and chaos. Investigators and the judiciary, along with their European colleagues, are working to determine who is behind them." Schools in France, Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Scotland also received similar emails this week. None of the respective police forces believed the threats were legitimate. Hundreds of schools across the Republic of Ireland received the emails, as did news organizations such as RTÉ, which evacuated its Donnybrook campus, disrupting scheduled programming. Around 300 schools in Northern Ireland received bomb threats, although the PSNI said these were being treated as a hoax, and that the risk to the public was deemed low. Likewise, Police Scotland confirmed around 1,000 schools were affected by the email campaign and that the threats weren’t believed to be credible. In France, three school districts confirmed they received similar threats. Separately, domestic and international rail travel, including Eurostar services to London, were interrupted on Thursday following bomb threats made to Calais-Fréthun station. The latest wave of threats follows similar happenings at other types of organizations in recent weeks, including airline operators, air traffic controllers, and blood banks. At least 34 flights across various operators in Europe were affected earlier this month. Some were forced into unplanned landings, such as an Aer Lingus flight which pulled up to a French air base instead of its intended target of Rome. Military fighter jets were also scrambled to escort others in Italian and Austrian airspace. ®

item.title: HPE debuts hybrid storage configs: Rising SSD costs hit supercomputing
item.description: HPE is pitching high performance compute customers with hybrid configurations of its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems built for faster throughput, along with a Rack Management Controller that monitors cooling systems. The hardware giant already supplies its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 in all-flash, all-disk, tiered and hybrid configurations, but - we're told - the latest combination offers up to 41 percent more data throughput per storage rack. The E2000 line embeds the Lustre open-source parallel file system, and is generally intended to fit NVMe Gen 5 solid-state drive (SSD) building blocks. For the refreshed hybrid configurations, HPE is combining SSDs with new 32 TB SAS-4 (24 Gb/s SAS) HDDs and new enclosures supporting 74 or 100 drives. HPE says it'll deliver up to 116 GB/s of read throughput and 92 GB/s of write throughput per rack, with up to 32 percent more usable storage capacity per rack for expansion to support the growing size of datasets in HPC, especially where sites are mixing AI and traditional simulation-style workloads. One of the reasons behind these new hybrid configurations could be the ballooning cost of storage, caused by the relentless demand for AI infrastructure skewing the price of components such as memory and many other things. But prices for silicon-based NAND flash SSDs are growing faster than those of good old hard drives , as our colleagues at Blocks & Files reported. HPE says that as demand for data-intensive workloads grows, prices for large SSDs have soared. The company claims the new hybrid configurations let research institutions and national laboratories spend less on storage and put that money toward compute node purchases, without giving up on the performance they need. “When making long-term investments in environments where advanced workloads are rapidly evolving, our customers want scalable, dense, and flexible systems to help them address dynamic shifts in requirements," said Trish Damkroger, HPE senior veep for HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions. The latest hybrid configurations are expected to go on sale in early 2027. HPE's other introduction is a Rack Management Controller, providing what HPE calls "intelligent liquid cooling” via real-time monitoring, leak detection and automated control features. It integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software to gather telemetry and provide control. Several platform-specific versions will be offered, each tailored to different rack-scale systems. Support will launch with HPE's own Cray Supercomputing GX5000 infrastructure, naturally, with versions for Nvidia’s NVL72 and AMD’s Helion and Helios kit to follow. The Rack Management Controller will be available for HPE’s kit in March 2027, with support for AMD and Nvidia expected to follow in June. ®

item.title: Microsoft outage gives customers a crash course in dependence on Redmond
item.description: Microsoft 365 services are slowly recovering from a prolonged outage that has handed critics of single-vendor dependence a particularly unwelcome case study. Ever wondered what it would be like if your IT supplier abruptly pulled the plug? Perhaps the result of a mood swing by an unpredictable political leader? For affected Microsoft customers, the disruption has offered an unwelcome preview. Email? Gone. Messaging with Teams? Iffy. Collaboration? Nope. The list of problems in what Microsoft delicately called a "Service Degradation" is breathtaking. The company put the incident's start at 1826 GMT on November 12. Exchange Online fell over. Viewing recently used files in the Microsoft 365 application was problematic. Copilot threw a wobbly. Microsoft 365 Education was affected (unfortunate, considering the changes the company has made ), and so on. At 1401 GMT on November 13, Microsoft reported: "We're continuing to see improvements in service availability," but the damage has surely been done. If the outage halted work at your organization, then questions will have to be asked. Even Microsoft's rivals had some sympathy for the engineers and administrators dealing with the problems. Jos Poortvliet, co-founder of Nextcloud, told The Register : "Mistakes happen in the IT industry. This holds true for companies of all sizes, including us. Our heart goes out to all the admins today. "This incident shows how dependent organizations are on a single ecosystem. Especially in critical infrastructure, monopolies are increasing the risk of stalling businesses globally if an incident occurs. "When everything is hanging on a single vendor, companies can't switch providers quickly to get back up and running, or have a second setup as backup, or pull the plug when under attack and keep working air-gapped." Similarly, Civo CEO Mark Boost noted that IT whoopsies were a way of life. "Every technology provider will experience failures," he said. "The real concern isn't that Microsoft has suffered an outage. It's that we've allowed so much of our critical infrastructure to become concentrated in the hands of so few companies, creating enormous single points of failure." Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, also commented: "The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK's digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services." This week, Microsoft warned users to treat its unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 as " permanently vulnerable ." Moving to Exchange Online brings its own dependencies, however. Beyond any compensation claims, Microsoft may face awkward conversations about those dependencies when contracts come up for renewal. And there are alternatives. item.title: Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload
item.description: Arm's Lorenzo Stoakes isn't quitting Linux kernel development, though he's stepping back from some of the patch-review work he used to handle. Stoakes is a principal software engineer at Arm and he's a busy chap. Aside from writing the forthcoming book The Linux Memory Manager , in his CV [PDF], he says: "I hold four maintainerships: memory mapping, memory mapping (locking), memory mapping (madvise) – essentially the entirety of the userland API to memory management – and the reverse mapping which connects physical to virtual memory." Even so, he plans to soon be doing a little less. Earlier this week he posted an email to the Linux kernel mailing list to say that he was planning to drop some of his workload. He explained: "Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain. […] Apologies for doing this, but given the current trends I'd like to do something to make my inbox a little more manageable." As it happens, this came just the day after the Paramount Penguin himself said that he saw signs that the AI patch tide was "starting to turn." Stoakes told The Register : "I am retaining my maintainerships and have no plans on giving those up, I just want my inbox to be less horrendous. "And yeah, AI is part of the reason; in general, it's gone from 'once a week' to 'daily' to 'half of what I see in review'. "But the AI wave is hitting [memory management] across the board, really." He added: "I have a habit of burning myself out over weekends and evenings – you can see my involvement on a thread talking about that here - which gives you a sense of my views if you read back through that thread." At the Open Source Summit last month, the Reg FOSS desk joined the "Ask the Expert" session with Greg Kroah-Hartman , and he too expressed worrying sentiments: "The onslaught of the LLM-generated patches… we don't have enough people to review them all… We need more reviewers. We don't have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years." Kroah-Hartman also said: "I want to go down to two Long Term Support releases – four, maximum. Six is too many. We're too busy. We don't have the manpower. It’s crazy." On Red Hat's model of offering 10 years of support for products with a given version of the kernel: "Debian does it right. Debian and Yocto run the world. I've argued for years that the RHEL and SLES model is broken. That's why I don't work for SUSE any more." ®

item.title: Most affairs don't matter except to the people involved. Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen's blunder will rock the world
item.description: It's a story as old as time. Billionaire nerd boy meets girl. Girl is later suspected of being a spy. News at 11. Oh, and it's also been reported that he was having an affair with one of his direct-report employees. When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a "romantic" blunder, he doesn't do it halfway. The boss of the world's most valuable company – well, it was until recently, anyway – publicly resigned yesterday, November 12, as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately. We don't know if he jumped or if he was pushed. He left after admitting to having an affair. Although he never named an affair partner, one of the affairs was reported to be with Alice Huang, AKA Huang Le. She's head of the Chinese company Megaspeed, which was an Nvidia partner. Megaspeed is accused of being a front for China's government that was used to transfer Nvidia chips to China, although this hasn't been proven. Some US officials also suspect [PDF] she's working for Chinese intelligence, although the DoJ said it hasn't yet reached a conclusion about this. The final nail in Jensen's coffin came when The New York Times reported he had also allegedly had an affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Jeeze, guy! In the aftermath, Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, was appointed interim CEO. She won't, I suspect, be in the job for long. CFOs are not CEOs. The jobs aren't remotely the same. In most companies, Huang would be replaced by the COO. That can't happen here. Nvidia doesn't have a COO. Both inside and outside of Nvidia, Huang is seen as Nvidia, and Nvidia as Huang. These days, billionaire CEOs are perceived as God-kings who know all and rule all. Much more often than not, that's BS. That isn't the case with Nvidia. Huang co-founded Nvidia on April 5, 1993. He was appointed CEO on day one, and he never left the job. At first, the company staggered forward. When it released the GeForce 256 in 1999 , which it marketed as the first GPU, it started on its path to becoming the chip manufacturer of choice for PC gamers. It still is today. That's a great niche, but it doesn't make a company a trillion-dollar business. No, the path to that dizzying height came when, in 2006, Nvidia unveiled CUDA . This programming architecture opened its GPUs' parallel-processing capabilities to scientific and other non-graphics workloads. From there, CUDA would become the foundation for most high-performance and AI computing. Huang was at the center of it all. He still was until now. At KubeCon North America , the trade show for Kubernetes, used in well over half of all AI projects, I spoke to many Nvidia employees. There were two things they all mentioned. Maybe the top brass and government officials both in China and the US knew Huang was fooling with fire; the developer rank-and-file folks I spoke to hadn't had a clue. item.dc:creator: Steven J. Vaughan-Nichols
item.content:encoded: It's a story as old as time. Billionaire nerd boy meets girl. Girl is later suspected of being a spy. News at 11. Oh, and it's also been reported that he was having an affair with one of his direct-report employees. When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a "romantic" blunder, he doesn't do it halfway. The boss of the world's most valuable company – well, it was until recently, anyway – publicly resigned yesterday, November 12, as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately. We don't know if he jumped or if he was pushed. He left after admitting to having an affair. Although he never named an affair partner, one of the affairs was reported to be with Alice Huang, AKA Huang Le. She's head of the Chinese company Megaspeed, which was an Nvidia partner. Megaspeed is accused of being a front for China's government that was used to transfer Nvidia chips to China, although this hasn't been proven. Some US officials also suspect [PDF] she's working for Chinese intelligence, although the DoJ said it hasn't yet reached a conclusion about this. The final nail in Jensen's coffin came when The New York Times reported he had also allegedly had an affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Jeeze, guy! In the aftermath, Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, was appointed interim CEO. She won't, I suspect, be in the job for long. CFOs are not CEOs. The jobs aren't remotely the same. In most companies, Huang would be replaced by the COO. That can't happen here. Nvidia doesn't have a COO. Both inside and outside of Nvidia, Huang is seen as Nvidia, and Nvidia as Huang. These days, billionaire CEOs are perceived as God-kings who know all and rule all. Much more often than not, that's BS. That isn't the case with Nvidia. Huang co-founded Nvidia on April 5, 1993. He was appointed CEO on day one, and he never left the job. At first, the company staggered forward. When it released the GeForce 256 in 1999 , which it marketed as the first GPU, it started on its path to becoming the chip manufacturer of choice for PC gamers. It still is today. That's a great niche, but it doesn't make a company a trillion-dollar business. No, the path to that dizzying height came when, in 2006, Nvidia unveiled CUDA . This programming architecture opened its GPUs' parallel-processing capabilities to scientific and other non-graphics workloads. From there, CUDA would become the foundation for most high-performance and AI computing. Huang was at the center of it all. He still was until now. At KubeCon North America , the trade show for Kubernetes, used in well over half of all AI projects, I spoke to many Nvidia employees. There were two things they all mentioned. First, they were in a state of shock. Maybe the top brass and government officials both in China and the US knew Huang was fooling with fire; the developer rank-and-file folks I spoke to hadn't had a clue. The second was that every month, Huang held an all-hands meeting where, instead of a per-forma corporate pep rally, he answered questions from everyone and gave them real answers. He knew his technology well and actually led his company instead of just impressing gullible stock buyers. Nvidia can't replace him. It really can't. I'm reminded of when John Sculley forced Steve Jobs out at Apple in 1985. If you're not old enough to remember, Apple did fine for a while, but then by the mid-90s, it lost its way. Apple got its mojo back, and started its rise to being one of the world's top companies only after Jobs came back in 1996 . The big difference, of course, is that Huang's not coming back. I heard many people say that Huang was "too big to fail." True, morality no longer matters much in the US – see Trump's kleptocracy – but this is different. Huang betrayed not just his wife, but his board, employees, and stockholders. If, as some suspect, the board knew full well what was going on, they should be tossed out too, but that's a story for another day. Oh, and as for Trump's suggestions that Apple's former CEO Tim Cook should become Nvidia's CEO? Give me a break. Now the question of the day is: how can Nvidia recover from this blow? I don't think it can. I used to say that I didn't know where the AI companies were going, but I was sure that so long as capital kept flowing into Big AI, Nvidia was the one company you could count on that would make money . I think I was wrong. What does that mean? In the short term, Nvidia stock, after dropping 14 percent in early trading on Thursday, is down "only" five percent. Despite all the Sturm und Drang over Huang's departure, the NASDAQ is actually, when I wrote this, up. Even Nvidia's bonds are holding steady . Amazon and Google, which have their own horses in the AI TPU races, are hoping, of course, that Nvidia's misfortune will help them lever open the AI hardware market. In these early hours, I don't see that happening. Frankly, I'm amazed at how stockowners are shaking off Huang's resignation. The AI fever dream, for now, is continuing unabated. That said, can this go on? This irrational exuberance rests on the belief that, no matter what happens, AI will continue to rule the stock market. Eventually, though, the bubble may pop, and that could put some strain on the global economy. For now, people are ignoring how bad this blow is, or perhaps they're not aware of it. In a few years, I expect Huang's affair will be seen as the first needle in the AI bubble. ®

item.title: Marlon Brando cool to Jensen Huang joke: how the black leather jacket became a meme
item.description: Once the ultimate symbol of Hollywood rebellion, the former Nvidia chief’s signature look is now being mocked as a midlife crisis cliche For nearly two decades a black leather jacket has been a key part of Jensen Huang’s look. Now it has become a punchline. As the founder and chief executive of Nvidia resigned this week after reports of multiple affairs, his affinity for a leather jacket, an item of clothing typically associated with a man in midlife crisis mode, has become widely mocked. Continue reading...

item.title: Oh my Word! Microsoft retires compatibility options, because who needs layouts to stay put
item.description: Microsoft is retiring some legacy layout settings in Word, potentially rearranging documents created or last saved in Word 2010 or earlier. "Affected documents may show layout differences, such as text reflow, changes in spacing or page count, or images and shapes moving to another page," the Windows biz said . The advice, if silly little things like page layout in a document matter, is to "consider exporting it to PDF before the change." Compatibility Mode lets a newer version of Word open a document created in an older version, such as Word 2010, without changing its layout. Newer features are switched off while the document is open this way. Users can convert the document to unlock newer features, although people using older versions of Word may then have difficulty editing parts of it. Microsoft has not identified the individual settings being retired, saying only: "We are retiring a set of compatibility options in Microsoft Word (desktop app) for documents in Compatibility Mode." The reason? "To simplify how Word handles document layout and provide a more consistent experience across platforms." Administrators may therefore want to check older templates, forms, and other documents whose pagination needs to stay put. The change is due to begin rolling out in the Windows version of Word from December 2026 and be completed by January 2027. The Mac version will follow in early 2027. Microsoft Word is more than 40 years old, and its first Windows version was released as the 1980s drew to a close. The word processor has evolved over the decades and is a mainstay of Microsoft's productivity suite. Compatibility Mode helps keep older documents from having their layouts abruptly borked the way Word does so well . Losing some of those safeguards could give administrators a fresh batch of "what the heck has happened to this document?" tickets as the change rolls out. ®

item.title: Quantum Systems drones back in the air after malware scare
item.description: Quantum Systems says its drones are flying again with Germany's military after a cyberattack prompted a precautionary grounding. The company says it spotted the attack at the end of October and reported it to the relevant authorities, but disclosed few details about the intrusion. "The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday. "Through the quick measures taken and the characteristics of the incident, there is no risk in operating Quantum Systems' unmanned systems for the end users and the operators." It added that other players in the European defense industry, and those who support Ukraine's military efforts, have faced "persistent cyberattacks for years." The Bundeswehr grounded its Quantum Systems drones after malware was detected in an update to QBase, the company's QBase ground-control software, Der Spiegel reported, citing unnamed sources. QBase lets operators plan missions, monitor flights, and process data from the ground. The malicious update reportedly reached servers belonging to the German military and other customers, but did not directly infect the drones. "The fleet is operating normally around the globe – including Germany and the Bundeswehr," Quantum Systems told Reuters . "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution." A spokesperson for Germany's defense ministry declined to comment on the attack or the reported details. The Register asked Quantum Systems for further details. Founded in 2015, Quantum Systems has been providing drones to the Ukrainian war effort for years. Last month, Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced funding for "several tens of thousands" of the company's interceptor drones as part of Germany's winter aid package. The new drones will be built in Ukraine and support interceptor systems already in use on the front lines. Quantum Systems announced a $1.2 billion Series D funding round in July, valuing the company at around $8 billion. ®

The Bundeswehr grounded its Quantum Systems drones after malware was detected in an update to QBase, the company's QBase ground-control software, Der Spiegel reported, citing unnamed sources. QBase lets operators plan missions, monitor flights, and process data from the ground. The malicious update reportedly reached servers belonging to the German military and other customers, but did not directly infect the drones. "The fleet is operating normally around the globe – including Germany and the Bundeswehr," Quantum Systems told Reuters . "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution." A spokesperson for Germany's defense ministry declined to comment on the attack or the reported details. The Register asked Quantum Systems for further details. Founded in 2015, Quantum Systems has been providing drones to the Ukrainian war effort for years. Last month, Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced funding for "several tens of thousands" of the company's interceptor drones as part of Germany's winter aid package. The new drones will be built in Ukraine and support interceptor systems already in use on the front lines. Quantum Systems announced a $1.2 billion Series D funding round in July, valuing the company at around $8 billion. ®

item.title: Palantir adds three UK police forces to its beat with £10.1M deal
item.description: Three UK police forces led by Cambridgeshire Constabulary have awarded Palantir a £10.1 million contract after London Mayor Sadiq Khan blocked a separate deal with the Metropolitan Police. The five-year agreement covers Bedfordshire Police, Cambridgeshire Constabulary, and Hertfordshire Constabulary, despite warnings from campaigners and politicians about dependence on the supplier. A contract award notice says the east of England police forces expect the Palantir platform to provide "an enterprise-wide data integration and analytics capability, enabling the secure ingestion, linking, and analysis of data from multiple systems and sources across the policing environment." The contract runs until October 2031, with the estimated value covering all three forces. News of the award coincided with revelations that former Metropolitan Police commissioner Dame Cressida Dick has worked as a paid adviser to Palantir since September 2025. A Palantir spokesperson told the Bureau of Investigative Journalism : "Dame Cressida is advising us on how our software could help improve the delivery of services in the public sector, drawing on more than 40 years of public service in a variety of roles." Dick said her role was limited to advising on how such products could assist public services. She said she had never lobbied or advocated for Palantir, or introduced the company to her contacts. Dick led the Metropolitan Police, the UK's largest force, between 2017 and 2022. She left after Khan said he had lost confidence in her. She later said she was " intimidated " into leaving. Separately, Khan stepped in to block the Met from awarding a £50 million contract to Palantir. His office cited serious concerns about the procurement process. Palantir later sued the Met, but the case was settled in October. The new police contract award follows a report from MPs warning of vendor lock-in to US suppliers, including Palantir. It said : "Our view that Palantir's increasing presence across the public sector represents an unacceptable point of weakness is not ideologically motivated or driven by concerns about the quality of their products. "The government should retain the ability to pick and choose individual suppliers and safeguard against the risk of vendor lock-in and debilitating dependencies, particularly in areas of critical national importance such as healthcare and national security infrastructure." ®

item.title: BOFH: The best way to stop an idea spreading is a controlled burn
item.description: Look, off in the ether – is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it's a stupid idea, on final approach... And look, the Boss has his office door open! C L E A R A N C E T O L A N D ! ... The Boss has wandered into Mission Control with something obviously on his mind. Over time, the PFY and I have learned to equate these thoughtful moments with the BAG FULL lamp of a commercial vacuum cleaner at a waxing salon. Do not open. His presence in Mission Control is never a good sign, but his "thoughtful" presence, even more so. He'll have seen something, read something, spoken to someone, or possibly overheard something in a toilet stall that will have sounded – to him – like a great idea. Or it might have been a cheddar-frenzy-induced fever dream that he wants to run by us. And the Boss's crazy ideas are, unfortunately, like bran flakes to his mental digestion, the output of which being delivered to the PFY and myself as a veritable slurry of poorly considered ideas. "AI," he says, pausing for effect, once he's rolled to a stop. He then waits patiently for one of us to ask "What about AI?" However, that will never happen. In terms of stupidity, it's up there with saying Candyman into a mirror five times, power washing a gremlin, or visiting a basement when Jason's in town. ... "For the security system," the Boss teases. I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same. The PFY and I know that the only way out of this is to stall till the end of the day, at which time the Boss's overnight reset will trigger, leaving him only a vague memory of having had a good idea. >clickety< >tap< "Uh-oh," I say, reaching into my drawer for my crashtop. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed." >tappity< "And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too." "It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to. "A virus?!" the Boss gasps. "I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing. ... So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him. Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow... >tappity< >tap< >tap< >clickety< On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously. >tappity< >tap< The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight. On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling. >bip< >bip< >bip< >biiiiiiip< >ring< "Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback. "It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the buildi

"For the security system," the Boss teases. I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed." >tappity< "And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too." "It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to. "A virus?!" the Boss gasps. "I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing. ... So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him. Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow... >tappity< >tap< >tap< >clickety< On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously. >tappity< >tap< The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight. On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling. >bip< >bip< >bip< >biiiiiiip< >ring< "Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback. "It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the building!!!" Meantime, I've messaged the PFY and advised him to pick up the shredder from the boardroom cupboard. "What do I do?" the Boss gasps. "It's the wireless broadband connection on the roof!" I say. "We need to disconnect it!" "I thought you said it was coming from inside the building?" the Boss asks. DAMMIT! >tappity< >click< >tap< >tap< Further discussion is impossible now that his phone is erasing itself, having been marked as a stolen device... The PFY was unable to find the shredder, as it looks to have been dumped now that board papers are no longer printed. On the plus side, he has a plan. ...two hours later... "So, we're clear to enter the building?" I ask the fire warden. "Yes, you're clear, though it looks like the fire started on your floor." "It doesn't surprise me," I say. "We're creative people. "Oh," I say, thinking of the smokers the PFY occasionally chats to outside at the skip. "Well, we may never know." "Don't you have some sort of AI surveillance system?" he asks. "Sadly, that was the first thing to go," I lie. ...Later, in Mission Control... "So, in review," the PFY says. "We shut down a couple of switches, put the building in night mode, trashed a laptop and a mobile phone, then set fire to the building." "Yes." "Simply to stop a dumb idea?" "Yes." "And the funny thing is, I took a look at his scribblings – and it wasn't all that bad." "Really?" I ask, reaching for the isopropyl and a lighter, just in case it's contagious. item.title: Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year
item.description: Britain's privacy watchdog has put healthcare bosses on notice after receiving more than 300 reports of staff snooping through medical records this year, demanding that executives personally confirm they're doing enough to keep prying eyes out of patient files. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said on Thursday that it had written to more than 200 senior health leaders across the UK, warning that employees accessing records without good reason put patient privacy and public trust at risk. The ICO received and assessed more than 300 reports of medical record snooping between January and mid-October 2026. Staff were caught looking up people they knew, poking around patient files out of sheer curiosity, and sharing private information with people who had no business seeing it. The figure covers reports submitted by healthcare organizations rather than confirmed breaches, and excludes cases still awaiting assessment. ICO chief executive Paul Arnold wants health bosses to personally assure him that their organizations have safeguards in place to stop staff having a nose through records they aren't supposed to see. "Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardize the vital trust people place in our health service," Arnold said. In a three-page letter to chief executives, Arnold makes clear that simply trusting staff to behave themselves won't cut it. He wants to know who can access patient records, whether anyone is checking what they're looking at, and what happens when somebody gets caught snooping. Health bosses are also expected to investigate suspected breaches without dragging their feet, work out whether patients need to be told, and take action against staff caught accessing records they shouldn't. Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order. The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news. This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison. That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't. Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order. The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison. That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't. Some newer electronic patient record systems can even flag suspicious access in real time, although the NHS acknowledged that monitoring capabilities vary depending on the technology organizations have installed. The scale of the problem has been troubling regulators for years. In July, the UK government told Parliament that 1,445 cases of inappropriate access had been reported to the ICO between 2019 and 2025. And the consequences can go beyond getting the sack. The ICO has prosecuted 16 healthcare workers for snooping through patient records over the past decade, with unauthorized access to personal information potentially amounting to a criminal offense under the Data Protection Act 2018. Arnold warned that the regulator could also take enforcement action against healthcare organizations whose protections aren't up to scratch. "I've written to chief executives across the UK asking them to personally assure me that their safeguards work in practice. Where they don't, we expect organizations to put that right," he said. With hundreds of reports already landing on the watchdog's desk this year, healthcare bosses now have a fortnight to explain how they're keeping staff out of records they have no business reading. ®

item.title: Farewell, Cybertruck: why the winding down of the ‘Maga hat on wheels’ is a sign of the times
item.description: Eccentric and overhyped, Tesla’s Cybertruck became a stand-in for Elon Musk during his ascent in the Republican party. It will join the ranks of other vehicles symbolic of their eras – for better or for worse Three days after a historic blue tsunami changed America’s political landscape, Elon Musk announced Tesla would end production of its hulking Cybertruck next year. Was it a coincidence? Maybe. Musk said the move was “to make room for increased Cybercab production”, referring to Tesla’s Robotaxi. But the combined circumstances felt highly appropriate: it was the end of an era. Continue reading...

item.title: Brit police watchdog says cops' use of facial recog risks wrongful arrests
item.description: UK police forces must do more to prevent the wrongful arrests of people subjected to retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches, according to a Criminal Justice Inspectorate that holds deep concerns about the way in which the technology is used. According to a report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), there is a large gap in understanding among police forces and the National Crime Agency about how RFR should be used in responsible policing. The inspectorate blamed "fragmented and underdeveloped" frameworks for governance and legislation. It pointed to a lack of bespoke legislation to provide a uniform approach to police facial recognition use – and said existing laws have not kept pace with the technology. HMICFRS also said the rules governing each force's use of RFR are mismatched, and called for a statutory code to be included in the forthcoming Police Reform Bill to set nationwide standards. Illustrating the breadth of misunderstanding across forces, the report noted that despite the message being routinely communicated by National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) reps, individual investigators "often" thought RFR results constituted evidence rather than intelligence. In many cases, they are unaware that RFR results require further enquiries before enforcement action can be taken. "We found that some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches," the report stated. "In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action. "Although some forces had strengthened their processes after such incidents, practice remained inconsistent." Later in the report, the inspectorate described the findings as "deeply concerning." Some of the excuses police staff offered included acute demands on response teams leading to reduced opportunities to carry out further enquiries before acting on RFR matches. In one force, managers were known to encourage officers to "progress investigations quickly" after getting a match on the RFR system. However, the inspectorate clarified that just because an arrest is made, it does not necessarily mean it is wrongful, as investigators may need to rule out subjects from their inquiries. The onus for taking action should also be placed on the police forces themselves, given that some lack formal procedures regarding how RFR enquiries should be carried out, the report noted. The best forces had centralized facial recognition teams, which generally provided better governance and consistent processes. Officials fear long-term misuse of RFR, and other forms of facial recognition, will erode public trust in the technology, which it insists remains generally high. item.dc:creator: Connor Jones
item.content:encoded: UK police forces must do more to prevent the wrongful arrests of people subjected to retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches, according to a Criminal Justice Inspectorate that holds deep concerns about the way in which the technology is used. According to a report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), there is a large gap in understanding among police forces and the National Crime Agency about how RFR should be used in responsible policing. The inspectorate blamed "fragmented and underdeveloped" frameworks for governance and legislation. It pointed to a lack of bespoke legislation to provide a uniform approach to police facial recognition use – and said existing laws have not kept pace with the technology. HMICFRS also said the rules governing each force's use of RFR are mismatched, and called for a statutory code to be included in the forthcoming Police Reform Bill to set nationwide standards. Illustrating the breadth of misunderstanding across forces, the report noted that despite the message being routinely communicated by National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) reps, individual investigators "often" thought RFR results constituted evidence rather than intelligence. In many cases, they are unaware that RFR results require further enquiries before enforcement action can be taken. "We found that some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches," the report stated. "In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action. "Although some forces had strengthened their processes after such incidents, practice remained inconsistent." Later in the report, the inspectorate described the findings as "deeply concerning." Some of the excuses police staff offered included acute demands on response teams leading to reduced opportunities to carry out further enquiries before acting on RFR matches. In one force, managers were known to encourage officers to "progress investigations quickly" after getting a match on the RFR system. However, the inspectorate clarified that just because an arrest is made, it does not necessarily mean it is wrongful, as investigators may need to rule out subjects from their inquiries. The onus for taking action should also be placed on the police forces themselves, given that some lack formal procedures regarding how RFR enquiries should be carried out, the report noted. The best forces had centralized facial recognition teams, which generally provided better governance and consistent processes. Officials fear long-term misuse of RFR, and other forms of facial recognition, will erode public trust in the technology, which it insists remains generally high. Surveys carried out in 2025 by the likes of the Ada Lovelace Institute and Alan Turing Institute , as well as the King's College London Policy Institute , showed a generally favorable view of facial recognition use in UK policing, with support ranging from 91 percent and 53 percent respectively. Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative experience. The Register's comments section often paints a vastly different picture of public perception of facial recognition. Kathryn Stone, his majesty's inspector at HMICFRS, said facial recognition has transformed policing, allowing officers to compare images in seconds, allowing them to solve crimes more quickly, but echoed the report's main concerns. "Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment," she said. "A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence." As well as legislative and governance-related concerns, HMICFRS also noted in its report that officers' training around the use of RFR remains inconsistent, and if improvements were made, this would lead to more effective and lawful use of RFR across the UK. Another major issue was police forces' failure to meet their image retention obligations. Forces were found too often to retain custody images taken of suspects on the Police National Database, against which many RFR queries are made. Police guidance sets out the scenarios in which custody images can and cannot be retained, and the inspectorate found that forces have failed to delete images that should have been wiped. The Police Reform Bill includes a provision to group custody images with the likes of DNA and fingerprints, bringing about more robust measures to ensure they are retained or deleted in line with legal requirements. A Home Office review previously found in 2017 that introducing such a statutory framework was untenable. It concluded that police could not automate the deletion of these images, and doing so manually would be too time-consuming. Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, said UK police cannot be allowed to continue to use RFR when it risks wrongfully arresting individuals . "The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming," she said. "This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they've never visited , as we've seen before. "Worse still, police aren't even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without any record of why they've been accused." Chaggar called on the government to "urgently step in" and help the UK's police forces to sort out the new frameworks needed for effective RFR use. ®

item.title: Palantir's NHS cancer app gets plenty of praise, precious few users
item.description: Only a handful of NHS trusts are using the cancer app on the controversial £330 million Federated Data Platform (FDP) run by Palantir, while newly released figures raise questions about which trusts are benefiting. Cancer 360 was designed to bring cancer patients' data from disparate spreadsheets and electronic health records into a central system, helping health professionals prioritize treatment. Pilots began four years ago, and trusts are not charged directly for the FDP. Yet official figures put Cancer 360's uptake at just five or six trusts. Freedom of Information responses gathered by grassroots campaign group No Palantir in the NHS also reveal discrepancies between reported benefits and recorded use. In June 2025, NHS England said that Cancer 360 "drastically cut down diagnosis times" and referred to a pilot at Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust, which saw the proportion of patients diagnosed within 28 days climb from 72 percent to 85 percent. The trust began trials in 2022, while working with Palantir under a £23 million contract awarded without competition, before the US firm was awarded the FDP contract in late 2023. Critics argued the FDP procurement was flawed as Palantir had developed use cases under £60 million in non-competitive contracts which were then carried over to the FDP. Last year, NHS England said Cancer 360 served 46 registered teams and 239 active users, and processed 52,000 patients. In June 2026, NHS England said there were five trusts using Cancer 360 as of March 2026. Of those, only two were listed as benefiting. In July, health minister Preet Kaur Gill repeated the five-trust usage figure in a Parliamentary answer . Official data released in October said that as of June, six trusts were using Cancer 360 and five were benefiting, but did not identify the trusts or explain the increase. The stats have since been removed from the NHS England website but are archived here . In June, NHS England responded to a Freedom of Information request . It said six trusts reported unique users logging into the Cancer 360 app over the last 12 months. However, two trusts cited as having run successful pilots – Chelsea and Westminster Hospital and Royal United Hospitals Bath – were listed as having zero unique users logging into the system during that period, according to NHS England's reply. Both trusts were said to have received benefits from the system, according to a FoI response sent to campaign group Foxglove in June this year. The Register asked both trusts and NHS England to explain the discrepancy. One of the six trusts said to be logging into the cancer app, East Lancashire Hospitals, reported just one unique user. It later confirmed in an FoI response in August that it was not live with the FDP. It had planned to adopt the platform, leading with Cancer 360, but did not have a date for going live with the app. No Palantir in the NHS also identified trusts that considered Cancer 360 but decided against adopting it.

In June 2026, NHS England said there were five trusts using Cancer 360 as of March 2026. Of those, only two were listed as benefiting. Official data released in October said that as of June, six trusts were using Cancer 360 and five were benefiting, but did not identify the trusts or explain the increase. The stats have since been removed from the NHS England website but are archived here . In June, NHS England responded to a Freedom of Information request . It said six trusts reported unique users logging into the Cancer 360 app over the last 12 months. However, two trusts cited as having run successful pilots – Chelsea and Westminster Hospital and Royal United Hospitals Bath – were listed as having zero unique users logging into the system during that period, according to NHS England's reply. Both trusts were said to have received benefits from the system, according to a FoI response sent to campaign group Foxglove in June this year. The Register asked both trusts and NHS England to explain the discrepancy. One of the six trusts said to be logging into the cancer app, East Lancashire Hospitals, reported just one unique user. It later confirmed in an FoI response in August that it was not live with the FDP. It had planned to adopt the platform, leading with Cancer 360, but did not have a date for going live with the app. No Palantir in the NHS also identified trusts that considered Cancer 360 but decided against adopting it. East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust considered using the app but rejected it because there was "no immediate requirement for it," according to its FoI response . In its FoI response , Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust said it did not adopt the app because of issues around the metadata requirements. Meanwhile, official figures on cancer diagnosis waiting times show wider improvements across England. Given Cancer 360's limited uptake, those national gains cannot simply be credited to the app. In July this year, the UK's statistical regulator told NHS England to ensure ministers are briefed accurately following a row over data used to promote the purported benefits of the Palantir-run FDP. Campaign group Foxglove had found that nearly a third of NHS trusts using Palantir's health data platform were performing fewer patient procedures than before it went live and that Chelsea and Westminster Hospital accounted for 84 percent of the reported fall in outpatient waiting lists, while only 16 trusts were using the FDP tool. The Office for Statistics Regulation began assessing NHS England's claims about the FDP's performance and the quango included more caveats on its website. Scrutiny of the FDP's reported benefits comes as the government decides whether to continue the Palantir-led contract beyond February 2027. The initial contract was provided for a term of up to seven years, with a maximum value of £330 million. Reports this week suggest the government is set to renew the contract , but run a parallel procurement to find an alternative to Palantir as pressure mounts to reduce lock-in to a single vendor and boost sovereign technology. Palantir was founded with startup money from a CIA-linked VC firm and has relied on close ties with the US intelligence, military, and immigration services since its inception, although its recent growth in the wider business market is notable. ®

item.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
item.description: CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe. It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability. item.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
item.description: Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade , it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia. After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP. Continue reading...

item.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
item.description: Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration Arriving alongside November’s blue wave , Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country , except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it. Continue reading...

item.title: Apple MacBook Pro review: lighter, thinner and a stunning OLED touchscreen
item.description: Redesigned flagship laptop has a fantastic display, killer performance and the first touchscreen on a Mac, but comes with a serious price tag Apple’s MacBook Pro has been redesigned for the first time in five years, getting slightly slimmer, significantly lighter and adding a fantastic new OLED display with the first touchscreen on a Mac. The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display comes in two sizes, 14in and 16in, but rather than replacing the standard MacBook Pro they sit alongside them as an even more expensive option. The OLED machines start at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) – a £400 or equivalent upgrade on the matching spec LCD models – serious prices for serious work machines, not helped by significant cost increases driven by RAMageddon . item.title: Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?
item.description: Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large. He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares. Continue reading...

item.title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked
item.description: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android Google’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out. For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/ $899 / A$2,299 ) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks. Continue reading...
